title: Deployments: blue-green, canary, feature flags, migrations, rollbacks
scopeHtml: Scope: Rolling, blue-green, canary, feature flags, expand-contract schema migrations, rollbacks, strategy choice.

notes.title: Deployment goals and the risk model
notes.html:
A deployment strategy decides how new code replaces old code while users keep using the system. The goals: zero (or near-zero) downtime, small blast radius when something is wrong, and a fast way back.

Two ideas drive every strategy:

  • Deploy is not release. Putting code on servers (deploy) and turning on behaviour for users (release) can be separated with feature flags.
  • Limit blast radius. Show new code to 1% of traffic first, so a bug hurts 1% of users for 5 minutes, not 100% for an hour.

Risk grows with batch size: a deploy with 1 small change is easy to reason about and revert; a release of 200 commits is not. That is why elite teams deploy many small changes per day (DORA research: change failure rate and time to restore are lower with small frequent releases).

Worked example. At 2,000 req/s with a 1% canary, 20 req/s hit the new version. If errors are 5% on the canary, only about 1 req/s fails; the alert fires within minutes and the canary is reverted. Same bug at 100% would fail 100 req/s.

Industry examples. Amazon deploys to production every few seconds across the company (reported publicly); Netflix uses Spinnaker with automated canary analysis (Kayenta); Facebook ships the web app multiple times a day with gradual exposure and flags; Etsy popularised continuous deployment.

Everyday analogy. Replacing the engine of a moving bus: you want a plan that never leaves passengers stranded, and a way to switch back if the new engine sputters.

Common interview traps.

  • Describing a strategy without naming the rollback path.
  • Treating all changes (config, code, schema) as equally risky.
  • Skipping the metrics that decide whether to continue or abort.

notes.title: Rolling deployments
notes.html:
A rolling update replaces instances a few at a time, so old and new versions run side by side during the rollout.

Kubernetes default (strategy: RollingUpdate) with 10 replicas, maxSurge: 25% and maxUnavailable: 25%: it adds up to 3 new pods, removes up to 2 old ones, waits for readiness, and repeats.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  replicas: 10
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 25%
      maxUnavailable: 0   # never drop below desired capacity
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: registry/api:2.4.1
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }
          periodSeconds: 5
        lifecycle:
          preStop: { exec: { command: ["sleep","10"] } }   # let LB drain
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

Key requirements:

  • Readiness probes so traffic only goes to pods that are ready.
  • Graceful shutdown: on SIGTERM stop accepting new work, finish in-flight requests (preStop sleep + grace period) otherwise users see 502s on every deploy.
  • Backward compatibility: old and new versions coexist, so APIs and DB schema must work with both.

Trade-offs. Cheap (no double capacity beyond surge) and the default. Slow rollback (roll forward again, same speed), and during the rollout you cannot tell cleanly which version caused a problem.

Decision gravity. Rolling is a reversible, low-effort default; the one-way part is whether your code tolerates mixed versions. If it does not, you need blue-green or a maintenance window.

Industry examples. Kubernetes Deployments, AWS ECS rolling updates, Amazon ASG instance refresh.

Everyday analogy. Replacing the carriages of a train one at a time at each station while it keeps running.

Common interview traps.

  • No readiness probe: traffic hits a pod that is still warming up.
  • Ignoring connection draining and long-lived WebSocket connections.
  • Assuming old and new never run together.

notes.title: Blue-green deployments
notes.html:
Blue-green runs two full environments: blue (current, live) and green (new). You test green, then switch all traffic from blue to green at once; rollback is switching back.

Mechanics: deploy v2 to green, run smoke tests against green with internal traffic, flip the load balancer target group / DNS / ingress selector, watch metrics, keep blue for 30 to 60 minutes (or longer) before decommissioning.

Switch options:

  • LB target group swap (AWS ALB listener rules): near instant, 0 DNS caching issue.
  • DNS weighted records: slow due to TTL and clients caching DNS (60 s TTL is often ignored by some clients).
  • Kubernetes Service selector change or Argo Rollouts blue-green.

Worked example. Service uses 20 pods (4 vCPU each). Blue-green needs 40 pods during the switch, so double the cost for that window. With cloud autoscaling the extra capacity exists for an hour, costing a small fraction of the monthly bill.

Trade-offs.

  • Pros: instant, clean rollback; test with production-like infrastructure before switching.
  • Cons: double capacity; shared resources (the database) are NOT duplicated, so schema changes must work with both versions; in-flight sessions and caches reset; all users switch at once (no gradual exposure).

Decision gravity. Good where instant rollback matters and the system is stateless. For stateful parts the database is the shared one-way door: both colours talk to the same DB, so migrations must be backward compatible (see migrations section).

Industry examples. AWS CodeDeploy blue/green, Elastic Beanstalk "swap environment URLs", Cloud Foundry, Argo Rollouts. Martin Fowler's description popularised the term.

Everyday analogy. Two identical stages in a theatre: set up the next play on the empty stage, then rotate the audience's view to it.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the shared database.
  • Saying blue-green is free; it needs double capacity.
  • DNS-based switching with long TTL leaving users on blue for minutes.

notes.title: Canary releases
notes.html:
A canary release sends a small slice of real traffic (1%, 5%, 25%, 100%) to the new version and automatically checks its health before expanding. Named after canaries in coal mines.

Gates compare canary vs baseline on: error rate, p99 latency, saturation, and business metrics (checkout conversion, crash-free sessions). Compare with a fresh baseline deployment of the old version, not the long-running fleet, to avoid cold-cache bias.

# Argo Rollouts canary with pauses and automatic analysis
spec:
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
      - setWeight: 5
      - pause: { duration: 10m }
      - analysis: { templates: [{ templateName: error-rate-and-p99 }] }
      - setWeight: 25
      - pause: { duration: 15m }
      - setWeight: 100

Choosing who is in the canary: random percentage, by region (smallest region first), by internal employees first (dogfooding), or sticky by user ID (so one user sees consistent behaviour). Use sticky assignment when a user flipping between versions would confuse them or corrupt state.

Worked example. 100,000 req/s globally. 1% canary = 1,000 req/s: enough to detect a 2% error rate within about a minute (20 errors/s), while a 0.01% rate would need much more time or traffic. Choose steps and wait times by traffic volume to get statistically meaningful data.

Industry examples. Netflix automated canary analysis (Kayenta, open sourced with Google); Google and Facebook release to a small datacenter or user group first; Android app staged rollouts on Google Play (1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, 100%) with crash-free rate watch; Istio/Envoy and AWS App Mesh do weighted routing.

Decision gravity. Canary is reversible (just set weight to 0) but needs good metrics and automation, which is the real investment. Compared to blue-green, it has the smallest blast radius but takes longer and needs mixed-version compatibility.

Everyday analogy. Restaurants testing a new dish on one table before putting it on the whole menu.

Common interview traps.

  • Canary with too little traffic to detect anything.
  • Comparing the canary to a long-warmed baseline.
  • Having no automatic abort; a human noticing at 3am is not a gate.

notes.title: Feature flags
notes.html:
A feature flag is a runtime switch that turns code paths on or off without redeploying. It separates deploy from release.

Types:

  • Release flags: hide incomplete work (trunk-based development), short lived.
  • Experiment flags: A/B tests with user bucketing.
  • Ops flags / kill switches: disable an expensive feature under load; long lived.
  • Permission flags: enable for a plan or a customer.
// Evaluate a flag with a stable user bucket and a safe default
fun isNewCheckoutOn(userId: String): Boolean {
    val rollout = flags.percent("new_checkout")          // e.g. 10
    val bucket = (murmur3(userId + ":new_checkout") and 0x7fffffff) % 100
    return bucket < rollout                              // same user -> same answer
}

Design points:

  • Stable bucketing: hash(user + flag name) so a user keeps the same experience as the percentage grows.
  • Default off and fail safe: if the flag service is down, use a cached last-known value or the safe default.
  • Local evaluation: SDKs download rules and evaluate in-process (microseconds), not a network call per check.
  • Clean up: stale flags become tech debt. Knight Capital (2012) lost about 440M USD in 45 minutes when old code behind a reused flag was activated on one un-updated server.

Mobile angle. On Android, flags fetched at app start (Firebase Remote Config, LaunchDarkly) allow turning off a broken feature in already-installed apps without waiting for a Play Store review. Keep fetch caching and defaults in the app; a server-side kill switch is a major safety net.

Decision gravity. Introducing flags is cheap and reversible; flag combinations grow (2^n states), so enforce expiry dates and owners. Build-vs-buy (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagsmith, Split) is a moderate decision; hide it behind an interface.

Industry examples. Facebook Gatekeeper, Flickr (early adopter of "flags" as continuous deployment tool), GitHub (Flipper), LaunchDarkly and Unleash.

Everyday analogy. A light switch wired in advance: the cables are installed (deployed) but the lamp stays off until you flip the switch (release).

Common interview traps.

  • Not removing old flags.
  • Per-request remote evaluation adding latency and a new failure point.
  • Random (non-sticky) assignment causing users to flip behaviour on every request.

notes.title: Database schema migrations without downtime
notes.html:
The database is shared by old and new code, so a schema change must work with BOTH versions during the rollout. Use the expand and contract (parallel change) pattern.

Steps to rename column fullname to display_name:

  1. Expand: add the new nullable column display_name. Old code ignores it.
  2. Deploy v2 that writes BOTH columns and still reads the old one (or reads new with fallback).
  3. Backfill existing rows in batches (e.g. 10,000 rows per batch with a pause) to avoid long locks and replication lag.
  4. Deploy v3 that reads only the new column.
  5. Contract: stop writing the old column, then drop it in a later release once rollback is no longer needed.
-- 1. Expand (fast, no table rewrite in modern Postgres for nullable column without default)
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN display_name text;

-- 3. Backfill in small batches
UPDATE users SET display_name = fullname
WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 10000 AND display_name IS NULL;

-- Build indexes without blocking writes
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_users_display_name ON users(display_name);

-- 5. Contract, much later
ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN fullname;

Dangerous operations (Postgres/MySQL examples; confirm per version):

  • ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT rewrote the whole table before Postgres 11; since 11, a constant default is metadata-only.
  • CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY blocks writes.
  • Adding NOT NULL or a foreign key validates the table under a strong lock; add as NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT.
  • Long ALTER waiting for a lock queues behind a long transaction and blocks all later queries: set lock_timeout (e.g. 3 s) and retry.
  • MySQL: use online DDL or tools such as gh-ost (GitHub) or pt-online-schema-change for big tables.

Worked example. Backfilling 200M rows in batches of 10,000 with a 100 ms sleep = 20,000 batches, around 33+ minutes plus query time; this avoids one 20-minute transaction that would block vacuum and spike replica lag.

Rollback. The point of expand-contract is that the code can be rolled back at any step because the old column still exists. Dropping data (contract) is the one-way door: do it only after the new version has been stable for days or weeks, with a backup.

Industry examples. GitHub gh-ost, Shopify's ghostferry and online migration practices, Stripe's four-step online migration write-up, Percona pt-osc, Django/Rails/Flyway/Liquibase tooling with "strong migrations" linters.

Decision gravity. Expand-contract costs 3 to 5 releases for one rename, a deliberate price for safety. Alternatives: maintenance window (simple, downtime), or versioned views. Destructive steps are one-way doors.

Everyday analogy. Building a new bridge beside the old one, moving traffic across, and only then demolishing the old bridge.

Common interview traps.

  • Renaming or dropping a column in the same release that stops using it.
  • CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY on a hot table.
  • Not setting lock_timeout, causing a lock queue outage.
  • Migrations and code deployed as one atomic step (they never are).

notes.title: Rollbacks, roll-forward and deployment safety nets
notes.html:
Rollback means going back to the previous version; roll-forward means fixing quickly with a new version. Both need to be rehearsed.

When rollback is easy: stateless code, backward compatible schema, flags to disable, artifacts for old versions retained, config versioned.

When it is NOT: after a destructive migration; after the new version wrote data in a format the old version cannot read; after external side effects (emails sent, payments charged); after a protocol upgrade (e.g. a new Kafka message schema that consumers cannot parse).

Safety nets:

  • Automated rollback on SLO burn: canary analysis aborts and reverts.
  • Kill switches via flags (fastest: seconds).
  • Immutable artifacts (container image tagged by git SHA), so rollback is kubectl rollout undo deployment/api.
  • Backward and forward compatible data formats: Protobuf/Avro schema rules (add optional fields only), tolerant readers.
  • Version skew testing in CI: run v(n) client with v(n+1) server and vice versa.
  • Deploy freezes at peak times and good deployment windows (not Friday evening).
  • Post-deploy verification: smoke tests and synthetic checks.
# Kubernetes quick rollback and history
kubectl rollout history deployment/api
kubectl rollout undo deployment/api --to-revision=17
kubectl rollout status deployment/api

Worked example. MTTR goal under 10 minutes: alert within 2 min (burn-rate page), human decides within 3 min, rollout undo takes 3 min for 20 pods with maxSurge 25%, verification 2 min. A flag kill switch would shave that to under 1 minute.

Real incident pattern. CrowdStrike (July 2024): a faulty content update was pushed to all endpoints at once without staged rollout; systems crashed on boot and could not self-recover. Lessons widely cited: staged rollout even for data/config updates, and make recovery possible without remote access.

Decision gravity. Make every release reversible by design; the places where you cannot (data deletion, external side effects) deserve extra review and slower rollout.

Everyday analogy. A climber's rope and anchors: you only move up once the last anchor held, so a slip never means a long fall.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming rollback is always possible.
  • Config and data changes bypassing the safe rollout process.
  • Rolling back code while the schema has already moved on.

notes.title: Choosing a strategy
notes.html:
Strategy Blast radius Rollback speed Extra capacity Needs mixed versions OK? Good for
Recreate (stop all, start new) 100%, with downtime Slow None No Dev, batch jobs, breaking changes
Rolling Grows during rollout Medium Small surge Yes Default stateless services
Blue-green 100% at switch Instant 2x Not during switch (only DB) Critical flip, simple stateless
Canary 1% then grows Fast Small Yes High traffic, risky changes
Feature flag Per user/segment Instant None Yes Decoupling release from deploy
Shadow (traffic mirroring) 0% users n/a Extra n/a Validating a rewrite with real traffic

Shadow / dark launch. Mirror a copy of production traffic to the new version and discard its responses (GitHub's Scientist library compares old and new results for refactors). Great for rewrites; beware side effects (the shadow must not send emails or charge cards).

Mobile apps. You cannot roll back installed apps. Use Play Store staged rollouts, force-update/min-version gates, flags with server kill switches, and backend backward compatibility for old app versions (often 6 to 12 months).

Industry examples. Etsy/Flickr (flags), Netflix (canary plus red/black deployments, their term for blue-green), Facebook (gradual rings), Google Play staged rollouts.

Common interview traps.

  • Picking one strategy for everything.
  • Forgetting that old mobile clients stay alive for months.
  • Shadowing traffic without disabling side effects.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Deploy is not release; use flags to decouple. Small, frequent changes reduce risk.
  • Rolling: default, needs readiness probes, graceful shutdown, mixed-version compatibility.
  • Blue-green: instant switch and rollback at 2x capacity; the shared database is the catch.
  • Canary: small traffic slice with automated metric gates; best blast-radius control.
  • Feature flags: stable bucketing, safe defaults, local evaluation, cleanup; kill switches matter for mobile.
  • Schema changes: expand, dual write, backfill in batches, switch reads, contract later; CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, lock_timeout, gh-ost for big MySQL tables.
  • Plan rollback before deploying; destructive data changes and external side effects are one-way doors.
  • Combine strategies (canary then flag ramp-up) and watch SLO burn to decide to continue or abort.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between deploying code and releasing a feature, and why does it matter for risk?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It shows whether you understand that risk control comes from decoupling, not from testing harder.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Deploy means the new binary is running on servers. Release means users can actually see the new behaviour. If I wrap new behaviour in a feature flag, I can deploy at 2pm on a Tuesday with the flag off, then release to 1%, 10%, 100% and turn it off in seconds if it breaks. Small batches plus separable release give a small blast radius and fast recovery.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Risk grows with batch size. A deploy of 1 commit is easy to reason about and revert; a release of 200 commits is not. So we want deploys to be boring and frequent, and releases to be deliberate and reversible.

commit -> CI -> image -> prod (flag OFF)   <- deploy, invisible
                         flag 1% -> 10% -> 100%   <- release, gradual
                         flag OFF                  <- rollback in seconds

Blast radius is the other lever: at 2,000 req/s a 1% exposure sends 20 req/s to new code. A 5% error bug fails about 1 req/s instead of 100 req/s.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Describing a strategy without naming the rollback path.
  • Treating config, code and schema changes as equally risky; schema is the one-way door.
  • Skipping the metrics that decide continue or abort.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does a flag not help? -> Schema changes, library upgrades and anything not behind a code branch.
  2. Why do small frequent deploys fail less? -> Fewer changes per deploy means an obvious suspect and a trivial revert (DORA findings).
  3. What does a flag cost you? -> 2^n state combinations, stale-flag debt, and a new runtime dependency; needs owners and expiry dates.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "flags let us turn things on and off". Senior: frames deploy and release as independent decisions, ties them to blast radius numbers, and names the cleanup and one-way-door costs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that bundle a big-bang Friday release find the failing change among 200 commits at midnight; teams with flags revert in a click.

questions.promptHtml: How does a Kubernetes rolling update work, and what must be true of the app for it to be zero-downtime?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many people know the YAML but not the failure modes that produce 502s on every deploy.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The Deployment replaces pods a few at a time, controlled by maxSurge and maxUnavailable. It starts new pods, waits for readiness, then kills old ones. For zero downtime I need a real readiness probe, graceful shutdown (stop accepting, finish in-flight, a preStop sleep so the load balancer drains), and code and schema that work with old and new versions side by side.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
With 10 replicas, maxSurge 25% and maxUnavailable 0, the controller adds up to 3 new pods, waits for each to be Ready, then removes old pods, never dropping below 10 ready.

strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 0 }
readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }, periodSeconds: 5 }
lifecycle: { preStop: { exec: { command: ["sleep","10"] } } }
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30

Why preStop sleep: endpoint removal and pod termination race; kube-proxy and the LB may still send requests for a few seconds after SIGTERM. Sleeping lets traffic drain first.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• No readiness probe, so traffic hits a pod still warming up.
  • Ignoring long-lived connections such as WebSockets; they are cut at termination.
  • Assuming old and new never run together.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is rollback slow? -> It is just another rolling update in reverse, same speed.
  2. How do you know which version caused errors mid-rollout? -> You cannot cleanly; tag metrics by version label.
  3. What if v2 changes a JSON field name? -> Mixed versions break; use expand-contract on the API or blue-green.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE recites maxSurge. Senior explains the SIGTERM/endpoint race, draining, and mixed-version compatibility as the real contract.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team saw a burst of 502s at every deploy for months; the cause was a missing preStop sleep, fixed with 3 lines of YAML.

questions.promptHtml: When would you choose blue-green over canary, and what does blue-green not protect you from?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know the shared database is the catch, and the cost side.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Blue-green gives an instant switch and instant rollback because the old environment stays warm, so I pick it when the flip must be atomic and the service is mostly stateless. It does not give gradual exposure, it needs double capacity during the window, and both colours share the same database, so schema changes must be compatible with both. Canary is better when I want a small blast radius and have good metrics.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mechanics: deploy v2 to green, smoke test, flip the target group, watch, keep blue for 30 to 60 minutes.

Users -> Router -> Green v2 (live)
         Router -> Blue v1 (idle, standby)

Switch options: ALB listener or target group swap (near instant), Kubernetes Service selector or Argo Rollouts, DNS weighted records (slow, TTL ignored by some clients). Cost: 20 pods at 4 vCPU become 40 during the window. Caches and sessions reset on green, so warm it before the flip.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the shared DB: rollback to blue after v2 wrote new-format data can break v1.
  • Calling it free; it is 2x capacity.
  • DNS switch with long TTL leaves users on blue for minutes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you reduce cold-cache shock after the flip? -> Warm green with replayed or mirrored traffic first.
  2. Can you combine blue-green with canary? -> Yes, shift weight on the router gradually between colours.
  3. Stateful sessions? -> Externalise sessions to Redis or JWT, otherwise users are logged out at the flip.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "two environments, flip the switch". Senior: names the DB as shared fate, the cost, cold-cache risk, and when canary beats it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A rollback to blue after a v2 migration that dropped a column turned a 1-minute revert into a 2-hour restore.

questions.promptHtml: How would you design feature flag evaluation so that it is fast, consistent per user, and safe if the flag service is down?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Flags become a hidden dependency in every request path; seniors design for that.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Evaluate locally in the SDK from a cached ruleset, not with a network call per check. Bucket by hash(userId + flagName) so a user's experience is stable as the percentage grows. Default off, and if the flag service is down use the last-known cached value or the safe default. Give every flag an owner and expiry so they are deleted.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
boolean isNewCheckoutOn(String userId) {
    int rollout = flags.percent("new_checkout");            // e.g. 10, from local cache
    int bucket = (murmur3(userId + ":new_checkout") & 0x7fffffff) % 100;
    return bucket < rollout;                                // same user, same answer
}
fun isNewCheckoutOn(userId: String): Boolean {
    val rollout = flags.percent("new_checkout")
    val bucket = (murmur3(userId + ":new_checkout") and 0x7fffffff) % 100
    return bucket < rollout
}

Including the flag name in the hash prevents the same 10% of users from being the guinea pigs for every experiment. Rules stream in via polling or SSE; evaluation costs microseconds. Types: release (short-lived), experiment, ops kill switch (long-lived), permission.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Per-request remote evaluation adds latency and a new failure point.
  • Random non-sticky assignment flips a user's behaviour on every request.
  • Never removing flags; Knight Capital lost about 440M USD in 45 minutes when old code behind a reused flag ran on one un-updated server.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you test 2^n combinations? -> You do not; keep flags independent, short-lived, and test the on and off path of each.
  2. Mobile angle? -> Fetch at app start with cached defaults; a server kill switch fixes installed apps without store review.
  3. Build or buy? -> Moderate decision; hide the vendor (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagsmith) behind an interface.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: an if statement reading a config. Senior: bucketing, local evaluation, failure defaults, lifecycle governance.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A flag service outage with fail-closed defaults turned every feature off at once and looked like a full outage.

questions.contextHtml: A checkout API runs 10 pods on Kubernetes. Every deploy produces a 20 to 40 second burst of 502 responses (about 1.5% of requests at 3,000 req/s) and then recovers. Error budget for the month is nearly gone. Deployment YAML: maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 25%, no readiness probe, terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30, no preStop hook. Load balancer logs show 502s from the ingress with upstream prematurely closed connection. The app handles SIGTERM by calling System.exit(0) immediately. The team suspects "bad code in the new version".
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix without changing the deployment strategy.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Roll back, the new version is buggy" or "increase replicas". It ignores that the errors happen on every deploy regardless of version, which points to the rollout mechanics.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does it happen on every version including trivial changes? (yes means mechanics). Are errors during startup or shutdown? Is there a long-lived connection type? What is startup time of the app?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Set maxUnavailable: 0 and slow the rollout to stop capacity dips; if a deploy is in progress, pause it with kubectl rollout pause.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) pods terminated while still receiving traffic (endpoint removal race, no drain); (b) new pods receive traffic before ready (no readiness probe); (c) app exits on SIGTERM with in-flight requests; (d) capacity drop with maxUnavailable 25%. Red herring: code bugs in v2.
  4. How I'd verify each: Correlate 502 timestamps with pod termination events (kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp); check pod start to first-200 time; kubectl rollout status while tailing ingress logs; compare request counts per pod.
  5. Root cause: Without readiness the Service sends traffic to starting pods that refuse connections, and on termination the pod dies before kube-proxy and the ingress stop routing to it. In-flight requests are cut by System.exit.
  6. Fix: Short term: add readinessProbe on /ready, maxUnavailable: 0, preStop: sleep 10. Long term: handle SIGTERM by stopping the listener, draining in-flight work, then exiting within the grace period.
  7. Prevention: A deploy-time synthetic test that hammers the service during rollout in staging; alert on 5xx rate per deploy; a platform template with these defaults.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not increase replicas hoping to dilute errors; not switch to blue-green for a 3-line fix. A longer preStop slows deploys slightly.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• WebSocket clients still drop? -> Send a close frame with a reconnect hint and jittered reconnect on the client.
  • Grace period too short for long requests? -> Raise terminationGracePeriodSeconds above the p99.9 request time.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A payments team chased a "flaky v2" for two weeks; every revision showed the same 1% spike. Three lines of YAML and a SIGTERM handler removed it, and the next five deploys were silent.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the code, scales up.
  • Hire: identifies readiness, drain and SIGTERM issues and fixes them.
  • Strong hire: also explains the endpoint-removal race, verifies with events and logs, and adds a deploy-time regression test.

questions.contextHtml: A video platform serves 100,000 req/s globally and 40 req/s on a niche admin API. The team wants "a 1% canary with a 10 minute bake" as company policy for both. Business tolerates about 0.1% error rate normally. A recent regression had a 2% error rate that nobody noticed on the admin API for hours. The canary comparison uses the long-running fleet as baseline.
questions.promptHtml: Is a blanket 1% canary right? How would you design canary gates per service?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Yes, 1% for everyone, it's standard." Ignores statistical power at low traffic and cold-cache bias in the baseline.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What metrics decide pass or fail? Is traffic bursty or diurnal? Is the user sticky? What is the cost of a bad minute for each service?
  2. Immediate mitigation: For the admin API, deploy to an internal-only slice first and add synthetic traffic.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: 1% of 100k is 1,000 req/s: a 2% error rate gives 20 errors/s, detectable in about a minute. 1% of 40 req/s is 0.4 req/s: a 2% error rate is one error every 2 minutes; 10 minutes yields about 5 errors, statistically meaningless.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compute required samples for the target effect size (for a 2% vs 0.1% shift, tens of failures needed); run a canary on a past known regression to see if the gate would have caught it.
  5. Root cause: One-size policy ignores traffic volume. Also comparing to a long-warmed fleet biases against a cold canary (cache misses look like latency regression).
  6. Fix: Scale step weight and duration by traffic: high-traffic 1% for 5 minutes then 10%, 50%; low-traffic services canary by time and synthetic probes, or use blue-green plus smoke tests. Compare to a freshly deployed baseline of the old version. Automate abort on burn-rate.
  7. Prevention: Per-service canary templates, a replay test of a known bad build, and metrics tagged by version.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not extend bake times to hours for everyone (kills deploy frequency). Do not use only error rate; add p99 and a business metric.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Users flip between versions and corrupt state? -> Use sticky assignment by user ID.
  • Gate flaps on noisy metrics? -> Require sustained breach over N windows and use a statistical test.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A low-traffic billing service passed a 1% canary with zero requests seen; the bug shipped to 100% and surfaced from customers.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts the blanket rule.
  • Hire: does the traffic math and adapts duration and steps.
  • Strong hire: adds fresh baseline, power analysis, and validates gates with a replayed bad build.

questions.contextHtml:
You review this migration that will run automatically in the same deploy as the code change, on a Postgres 14 orders table with 300M rows doing 4,000 writes/s. The deploy renames status to state, and the new code only reads state. Rollout is a 10-pod rolling update.

BEGIN;
ALTER TABLE orders RENAME COLUMN status TO state;
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN archived boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false;
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_state ON orders(state);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT fk_customer FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id);
COMMIT;
questions.promptHtml: List everything that will go wrong and rewrite the plan.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Notices only "rename breaks old pods". Misses lock behaviour, index build and FK validation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Postgres version (constant defaults are metadata-only since 11)? Long transactions or analytics queries on this table? Can writes pause? Rollback requirement?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Do not merge; if already running, check pg_stat_activity for blocked sessions and cancel the DDL.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) RENAME instantly breaks old pods still running v1 during the rolling update: errors for minutes. (b) CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY blocks writes on 300M rows, and cannot run in a transaction if made concurrent. (c) FK addition validates the whole table under a strong lock. (d) The ALTER queues behind a long transaction and blocks all later queries (lock queue). (e) Whole thing in one transaction holds locks for the total duration.
  4. How I'd verify each: Test on a production-size copy; watch pg_locks; EXPLAIN is not enough, time the DDL; check for long transactions in pg_stat_activity.
  5. Root cause: Treating code and schema as one atomic step; they never are. Old and new code coexist.
  6. Fix: Expand and contract: (1) add state nullable; (2) deploy code writing both, reading status with fallback; (3) backfill in 10,000-row batches with a pause; (4) CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY; (5) deploy code reading only state; (6) later drop status. FK as NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT. Set lock_timeout = 3s and retry. ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT false is fine on PG 11+ (verify version).
  7. Prevention: A migration linter ("strong migrations" style), separate migration release from code release, and review checklist for locks.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: It takes 4 to 5 releases for a rename; the price of safety. Do not choose a maintenance window unless the business accepts the downtime.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Backfill causes replica lag? -> Throttle by lag and use smaller batches.
  • Need to roll back after step 5? -> Still possible because both columns are populated until the contract step.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single ALTER waited behind a 20-minute report query; every subsequent query on the table queued behind it and the site went down for 9 minutes with zero CPU load.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only fixes the rename.
  • Hire: expand-contract, CONCURRENTLY, batching.
  • Strong hire: lock queue, NOT VALID, lock_timeout, version caveats and rollback at each step.

questions.contextHtml: At 14:05 a release of the orders service goes to 100% over 30 minutes. At 14:40 p99 latency rises and 3% of orders fail validation. On-call runs kubectl rollout undo at 14:45; pods revert, but errors rise to 8%. Findings: v2 started writing price_cents as a new Avro field into a Kafka topic and changed the DB column price to numeric(12,2) using a one-step ALTER; v1 consumers throw on the new schema. v2 also sent 1,900 confirmation emails during the window. Rollback took 6 minutes to execute. Error budget is burned.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: why did rollback make it worse, and what changes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "We should have tested more." Assumes rollback is always safe and gives no systemic fix.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was the change behind a flag? Did the schema registry enforce compatibility? Was the ALTER reversible? Did we have a canary?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll forward with a hotfix that tolerates both schemas, or stop consumers, pause the topic's producers, and fix data; do not keep flipping versions.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) incompatible data format already written (one-way door); (b) schema changed in the same release as code; (c) no staged rollout: 100% in 30 minutes; (d) side effects (emails) cannot be undone.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare schema versions in the registry; check consumer error logs; compare DB column type history; trace rollout timeline against error rate.
  5. Root cause: Rollback restores code, not data or external effects. The release crossed three one-way doors (Kafka schema, destructive column change, emails) without a safe path back.
  6. Fix: Short term: roll forward with compatibility shim. Long term: Avro/Protobuf rules (add optional fields only), expand and contract for the column, a registry compatibility check in CI, version-skew tests (v(n) with v(n+1)), kill-switch flag for the new path, canary with automated abort, and a side-effect guard (idempotency keys, dry-run mode).
  7. Prevention: Deployment checklist asking "what can't be undone?", slower rollout for steps with irreversible effects, and a rehearsed roll-forward runbook with an MTTR target under 10 minutes.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No blanket Friday freeze as the only fix; it treats symptoms. Do not assume rollout undo is the universal safety net.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Could we have rolled back faster? -> A flag kill switch would have been under a minute versus 6 minutes of pod churn.
  • Emails already sent? -> Send a correction and add a send-dedupe key; cannot unsend.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team learned that a protobuf field renumbering was undetectable by tests, and only a skew test in CI that ran an old client against the new server would have caught it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames lack of testing.
  • Hire: names one-way doors and compatibility rules.
  • Strong hire: delivers a blameless, systemic fix set with flags, skew tests, canary gates and a roll-forward runbook.

questions.contextHtml: An e-commerce site (50 pods, 4 vCPU each) does blue-green on AWS with a Route 53 weighted DNS record (TTL 60 s). At 10:00 the team flips 100% to green. By 10:03 green shows 2.5% errors and p99 of 4 s; they flip back at 10:04, but dashboards show blue still receiving only about 40% of traffic at 10:08 and green still receiving 60%. Green's cache hit rate is 12% against 96% on blue. Database CPU on the shared primary spiked from 30% to 85% at 10:01.
questions.promptHtml: What happened, and how would you redesign the cutover?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Green had a bug." It ignores the DNS TTL behaviour and cold cache, both visible in the numbers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is DNS the only switch available? Are clients JVMs or mobile apps with their own DNS caches? Did we warm green? Same DB for both colours?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Keep the weight on blue at 100% and accept that stragglers drain; scale blue if needed; throttle green traffic via an LB rule, not DNS.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) cold cache on green pushed 88% of reads to the DB (DB CPU 30% to 85%), causing latency; (b) DNS caching: some resolvers and clients ignore the 60 s TTL so rollback was slow; (c) a v2 bug; (d) shared DB saturation. Red herring: green pod CPU.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare cache hit ratios and DB query rates per colour; check dig answers across resolvers and client logs for the resolved IP; run v2 against a replay in staging.
  5. Root cause: Cold-cache stampede at a 100% instant flip, plus a slow DNS-based switch that also made rollback slow.
  6. Fix: Use an ALB target-group or listener-rule swap (near instant, no DNS caching); warm green with mirrored or replayed read traffic before the flip; shift in steps (10%, 50%, 100%) via weighted target groups; keep blue 30 to 60 minutes.
  7. Prevention: Cutover runbook with cache hit rate and DB CPU gates; warm-up job; alert on DB CPU per release.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Gradual shifting means mixed versions, so v1 and v2 must be compatible; that is the price. Do not just lower the TTL to 5 s; resolver compliance is unreliable.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not canary? -> If mixed versions are acceptable, canary is better; blue-green was chosen for an atomic cutover that turned out to be unnecessary.
  • Extra cost? -> 100 pods for an hour is a small fraction of the monthly bill.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A 60-second TTL record was still resolving to the old environment for 11 minutes for a subset of corporate networks, so the "instant rollback" was not.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the build.
  • Hire: spots cold cache and DNS TTL.
  • Strong hire: redesigns with LB swap, warm-up, stepwise weights and DB gates.

questions.contextHtml: Product asks: "We want a big red button to disable the new recommendations carousel in the Android and iOS apps if it misbehaves." The backend is a flagged feature already. The mobile apps have 8M DAU, 40% on versions older than 4 weeks, and a store review takes 1 to 3 days. The flag service SDK is called per screen render. Last month the flag vendor had a 25 minute outage; apps crashed because the SDK blocked on startup.
questions.promptHtml: Design the kill switch. What do you ask first and what would you build?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a flag in LaunchDarkly." Ignores old app versions, vendor outage, blocking startup and latency.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does "misbehaves" mean (crash, bad content, load on backend)? Maximum time to disable? Must it work offline? Do old app versions have the flag SDK at all? Who is allowed to press it?
  2. Immediate mitigation: For old versions without the SDK, disable server-side: the BFF stops returning the carousel so clients render nothing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: failure paths are (a) flag service down, (b) stale cache, (c) old clients, (d) flag read blocks UI. Design against each.
  4. How I'd verify each: Chaos test: block the flag endpoint in staging and check cold start and render; check version distribution by cohort; measure SDK evaluation time.
  5. Root cause (of fragility): Client flags with no cached default and blocking init made the vendor a hard dependency.
  6. Fix: Layered switch: (1) server-side kill in the BFF (works for every version), (2) client flag fetched async at startup with cache on disk and a safe default (carousel off if unknown for a risky feature), TTL 5 to 15 minutes, (3) local evaluation, never per-render network calls, (4) audit log, role-based access and a two-person rule for global flips, (5) a metric that shows how many clients have applied the new value.
  7. Prevention: Quarterly game day that flips the switch in production and measures time to effect (p95 under 15 minutes); SDK timeout 500 ms with non-blocking init.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Fail-closed defaults for risky features may hide it during a vendor outage; pick per feature. Not remote-config polling every few seconds (battery, load).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Vendor outage again? -> Cached rules plus a self-hosted fallback endpoint on our CDN.
  • Need effect in under 1 minute? -> Push via silent notification or a long-lived stream, with the cost of battery and complexity.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team discovered during an incident that only 55% of installs had received the new config in the first hour; the metric to see it did not exist.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "just add a flag".
  • Hire: client cache, defaults and server-side switch.
  • Strong hire: asks about the requirement, defines time-to-effect, tests with chaos and covers governance.

questions.contextHtml: A MySQL 8 events table has 2.4 billion rows (1.8 TB), 6,000 writes/s, with a replica for reads. You must change user_id INT to BIGINT because IDs will overflow in about 5 months. A plain ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY on a staging copy took 11 hours and rebuilt the table. Replica lag already hits 20 s at peak. The business allows no maintenance window.
questions.promptHtml: Plan the migration, and the numbers you would check.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run the ALTER at night." Misses table rebuild, replication lag and rollback.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it a primary key or just a column? Online DDL supported for this change (verify, a type widening usually rebuilds)? How much free disk (need roughly the size of the table)? Is the replica used for reads where lag matters?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not urgent; the deadline is 5 months, so we have time to be careful. Put a lag alert at 5 s.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Options: (a) native online DDL (copies the table, may still stall replicas), (b) gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change (shadow table, binlog tailing, throttle), (c) new table plus dual write plus backfill plus cutover.
  4. How I'd verify each: Rehearse on a production-size copy; measure copy rate: 1.8 TB at 50 MB/s effective is about 10 hours; check disk and binlog volume; test throttling on replica lag.
  5. Root cause (of risk): The rebuild writes 1.8 TB through the primary and replicas, doubling IO, and cutover needs a brief metadata lock.
  6. Fix: Use gh-ost with --max-lag-millis throttling, cut over in a low-traffic window with a short lock timeout; keep the old table (renamed) for rollback for a week; ensure application code handles BIGINT (Java Long, JSON, ID generators) before and after the change.
  7. Prevention: Monitor ID headroom (alert at 70% of INT max); use BIGINT from day one; linter for new tables.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: gh-ost costs time (about a day) but is pausable and reversible; a direct ALTER is faster but unpausable and risks a full rebuild with lag. Do not skip the rehearsal.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Lag climbs to 60 s mid-run? -> Throttle automatically, pause, and resume; the tool supports that.
  • Foreign keys on the table? -> gh-ost has limited foreign key support (verify); plan a dual-write approach instead.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An INT overflow at 2.147 billion stopped inserts for a whole product; the emergency ALTER ran for 14 hours of downtime.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: direct ALTER.
  • Hire: shadow-table tool with throttling and rollback.
  • Strong hire: capacity math, rehearsal, app-side type changes, FK caveat and early-warning monitoring.

questions.contextHtml: You own the release process for three systems: (1) a stateless pricing API at 20k req/s, (2) a rewrite of the recommendations engine that must be validated against real production behaviour before users see it, (3) a mobile banking app with 3M installs. Leadership wants "one deployment strategy to rule them all" to simplify the platform. Past incidents: bad config pushed to all clusters at once; a rewrite that passed tests but gave worse results in production.
questions.promptHtml: Choose strategies per system and defend the decision. How reversible is each choice?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Canary for everything." Ignores shadow validation, mobile constraints and config safety.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Mixed-version tolerance of the pricing API? Do the recommendations have side effects? How long do old mobile versions stay alive? What counts as a bad rollout (SLO numbers)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: First fix the config-push gap: config changes go through the same staged rollout as code.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Pricing: canary then rolling, with metric gates, because blast radius matters at 20k req/s. Recs rewrite: shadow (traffic mirroring) with a comparison library like Scientist, then a flag-based ramp. Mobile: staged store rollout (1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, 100%) plus min-version gate, flags with a server kill switch, and backend compatibility with old clients for 6 to 12 months.
  4. How I'd verify each: Pricing: canary vs fresh baseline on error rate, p99, price-diff metric. Recs: result diff rate, latency, and no side effects in shadow. Mobile: crash-free sessions and ANR rate per release.
  5. Root cause (of past incidents): One path for code with another for config; no production-parity validation for a rewrite.
  6. Fix: A platform with a shared pipeline (build once, canary, flag ramp) but strategy chosen by service tier, rather than one strategy. Shadow must disable side effects (no emails, no charges).
  7. Prevention: Golden-path templates, policy checks (CI rejects direct-to-100% rollouts), and quarterly review.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Blue-green for the pricing API only if mixed versions are impossible; shadow doubles load on downstreams; mobile cannot roll back installed apps so backward compatibility is the only real rollback. Strategy choice is mostly reversible; the data and API compatibility contracts are not.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Pricing needs atomic switchover (legal change at midnight)? -> Deploy dark, flip with a time-based flag, not a deploy.
  • Shadow shows 3% result differences, is that bad? -> Triage: expected improvements vs regressions, with sampling and manual review.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A rewrite validated by shadow found a 7% mismatch on a locale edge case that unit tests never covered; users never saw it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: one strategy for all.
  • Hire: matches strategy to system and names rollback paths.
  • Strong hire: includes config safety, shadow side-effect guard, mobile compatibility window and reversibility analysis.
